newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PMs ask King to pardon Ieng Sary.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PMs ask King to pardon Ieng Sary.

text.p: Cambodia's two co-premiers sent a letter to King Norodom Sihanouk seeking a pardon for dissident Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary for his role in the genocide of the 1970s, one of the premiers said.

"Yesterday, I and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen wrote and sent a letter to his majesty the king to ask for amnesty for Ieng Sary," First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Thursday at a pagoda opening in Kompong Speu province, neighbouring Phnom Penh.
Ranariddh had told reporters on Wednesday he expected the King to grant the amnesty.
Sihanouk had said on August 21 he would only consider granting amnesty to Ieng Sary after receiving written requests from the government and a two-thirds majority of the 120-member national assembly.

Ieng Sary, foreign minister during the Khmer Rouge's brutal 1975-79 rule of Cambodia, was sentenced to death in absentia for his role in the genocide of more than one million people during the Khmer Rouge reign of terror.
Talk of an amnesty arose after Ieng Sary broke last month with the guerrilla group's hardline leader Pol Pot.
Ieng Sary, who the hardline Khmer Rouge rebels now want to execute, has formed a group of thousands of breakaway rebels and is talking peace with the Phnom Penh government.
He has said he wants the government to clear his legal status before continuing reconciliation talks. His participation would enhance prospects for overall peace in Cambodia, analysts said.

Ranariddh also renewed his call for two other senior Khmer Rouge figures, nominal leader Khieu Samphan and defence chief Son Sen, to join the government, but reiterated that a pardon for Pol Pot was unacceptable.
"If we can give amnesty to Ieng Sary, we should consider seriously about (giving amnesty to) Khieu Samphan and Son Sen."

The prince also saluted Ieng Sary, whom he had last month described as unacceptable, saying: "Ieng Sary recognises 100 percent the government, the constitution, the parliament, the monarchy and Buddhism -- Long live Ieng Sary".

He also noted the dividends that would come with a peace deal. "If we can finish the war...we can transfer the funds to the ministries of education, rural development, agriculture and others to develop the country," he said.
Official figures put defence costs at about 20 percent of the national budget, but analysts believe the figure is higher.
